nameStory: The shark eye gets its name from its distinctive shell pattern that resembles the dark, piercing eye of a shark. When you look at the shell from above, the dark brown or purple spiral creates an eye-like appearance with a pale 'pupil' in the center. This striking resemblance to a predator's eye is fitting, since shark eyes are themselves fierce predators of the sandy seafloor.
description: The shark eye is a large, predatory sea snail that prowls New England's sandy ocean bottoms. Its smooth, rounded shell can grow as large as a tennis ball and ranges from pale gray to brown with distinctive dark spiral bands. Like other moon snails, it's a voracious hunter that uses its muscular foot to plow through sand in search of clams and other shellfish. When the animal is active, its enormous, fleshy foot can completely engulf the shell, making it look more like a blob than a snail.

idTips.label: Shell shape and size
idTips.description: Large, smooth, globular shell up to 3-4 inches across that feels heavy and solid in your hand, with a rounded, almost spherical profile

idTips.label: Eye-like pattern
idTips.description: Dark brown to purple spiral bands create a distinctive 'eye' pattern when viewed from above, with lighter areas forming the 'pupil'

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface that feels almost polished, without the rough ridges or bumps found on many other shells

idTips.label: Umbilicus opening
idTips.description: Large, deep navel-like opening (umbilicus) at the base of the shell that you can easily fit your fingertip into

idTips.label: Living animal
idTips.description: When active, the huge, pale, jelly-like foot extends far beyond the shell and feels slippery and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Base color ranges from pale gray to tan or light brown, often with a subtle bluish or purplish tint to the darker spiral bands

habitat: Shark eyes live on sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters from the low tide line down to about 100 feet deep. You'll find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches throughout New England, especially after storms. They prefer areas with soft sediment where they can easily burrow and hunt for buried clams and other mollusks.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells begin washing up on beaches as winter storms subside. Living animals become more active in warming waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding fresh, intact shells on beaches. Living shark eyes are most active in warm water, hunting in sandy shallows.
seasonality.fall: Continued shell washing as autumn storms stir up the seafloor. Animals begin moving to deeper water as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Fewer fresh shells found on beaches. Living animals retreat to deeper, more stable waters offshore during the coldest months.

funFact: Shark eyes are shell-drilling assassins that bore perfectly round holes through their victims' shells using a combination of acid and a file-like tongue called a radula - when you find a clam shell with a neat circular hole, you're looking at evidence of a shark eye's deadly dinner!
confusionNotes: Shark eyes are often confused with other moon snails, but their distinctive dark spiral 'eye' pattern and large size set them apart. Remember: if it looks like it's staring back at you with a dark eye, you've found a shark eye! Other moon snails tend to be more uniformly colored without the dramatic eye-like markings.
contextualKnowledge: Until 2006, scientists thought there was just one species of shark eye, but researchers discovered that what they thought was one species was actually two very similar ones. The 'true' shark eye (Neverita duplicata) and its close relative Neverita delessertiana are so alike that even experts need to examine them carefully to tell them apart.
compareHints: Since the shark eye is the only Neverita species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other moon snails in the family Naticidae. Shark eyes are distinguished by their larger size, distinctive eye-like spiral pattern, and the prominent deep umbilicus (navel opening) at the shell's base. Other moon snails in the region are typically smaller and lack the dramatic dark spiral eye pattern that gives this species its memorable name.
